etymology: From the statistical base rate: how common a thing is before you know anything else about the particular case.
committed_when: A vivid case is on the table and the question of how common it is has not been asked.
tell: The number of incidents is quoted and the population is not. The story is true, the inference from it is not, and nobody multiplies.
counter: Ask out of how many, and what the rate was before. A rise from two to four is a doubling and it is also two people.
senses: Judging the frequency of an event by the salience of one instance, or by a test result, while ignoring how rare the event was to begin with.

It works because the vivid case is the one that reaches you. Selection decides what you see, so the sample in your head is not the sample in the world - and the denominator is the part of the story that never travels.
example: “Three of them in one month.” Three out of how many, in a city of how many, against a five-year average of what?

confused_with.tell: Anecdotal evidence argues from one case; the base rate fallacy argues from one case while a rate sits unread beside it.
